book: 013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way

chapters.file: ch53 - I Can Become Something More.md
chapters.relation: Reads Batgirl: Year One as a story of moral perfectionism: Barbara Gordon stumbles into the Batgirl role at a costume ball and resolves that she 'can become something more,' needing Batman as an exemplar in the sense of Nietzsche's 'Schopenhauer as Educator' — not a model to copy but someone farther along who acknowledges the legitimacy of her desire for a higher self. Batman's question 'Why do you want to be one of us?' tests her self-knowledge, and her 'Because I can' wins her a chance; his unmasking at his parents' graves is his acknowledgment of her quest. The chapter stresses that an exemplar's path cannot be duplicated: Barbara's higher self must be rooted in her own unique experience and desire.

chapters.file: ch54 - There Is What Could Be.md
chapters.relation: Argues there is no single final 'best self' in the perfectionist quest: after the Joker shoots Barbara, Oracle: Year One has martial-arts teacher Richard Dragon ask 'Who are you?', and she emerges thinking 'I'm me — more me than I have ever been.' Against the conformity John Stuart Mill warned of, the chapter has Barbara leave Dick Grayson because he has 'managed to turn into Bruce' and keeps 'reminding me of what I once was' — the past acting as a retrograde exemplar and a Millian custom that blocks her next, still-unattained higher self.

chapters.file: ch55 - Of Like Minds.md
chapters.relation: Concludes the Batgirl study by asking who accompanies Barbara once the exemplar stage is past: friends as equals — Dinah Lance (Black Canary) and Helena Bertinelli (Huntress) — who listen with fresh ears, call her out, and provoke her growth rather than direct her. Barbara's attempt to bench Dinah, and Dinah's response of taking up new training, show friendship as mutual provocation toward a better self, capped by the move to the airborne Aerie One as an image of her 'unattained but attainable self.' Moral perfectionism is offered as a lens through which comics help us calibrate our own progress.

chapters.file: ch56 - Chapter 9 - Batman and Friends Aristotle and the Dark Knight’s Inner Circle.md
chapters.relation: Opens Matt Morris's chapter by asking whether Batman — more inner-solitary than Spider-Man or Daredevil, whose civilian alter egos enjoy ordinary friendships — could have or be a friend at all. It quotes Ecclesiastes and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics line 'Without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods,' as deployed in Loeb's Hush, to set up the analysis of Batman's inner circle of Robin, Alfred, and the rest.

chapters.file: ch57 - From Aristotle to the Bat-Cave.md
chapters.relation: Lays out the chapter's analytical tool: Aristotle's three kinds of friendship — utility (mutual practical benefit), pleasure (mutual enjoyment), and complete or virtue friendship between committed, roughly equal good people, 'one soul in two bodies.' Noting that the ancient Greek concept is broader than today's 'friend,' it then turns this threefold taxonomy onto Batman's closest relationships to see whether any rises to the highest form.

chapters.file: ch58 - Batman and Robin.md
chapters.relation: Applies Aristotle's categories to Batman and Dick Grayson: Robin receives training, gadgets, and a mission (utility) and enjoys the mentorship (pleasure), repaying the huge imbalance with the love and honor Aristotle says the lesser friend owes. Aristotle's claim that the young's pleasure friendships are unstable explains Dick's growth into Nightwing; their later renewed camaraderie as near-equals 'moves in the direction of a complete friendship, but never seems to arrive at quite that high a plateau.'

chapters.file: ch59 - The Bat, Harvey Dent, and Two-Face.md
chapters.relation: Treats Batman's bond with District Attorney Harvey Dent as a utility friendship built on shared, extralegal zeal for justice — until acid scarring turns Dent into Two-Face. Using Aristotle's rules that a virtue friendship must end with an incurably vicious person but not be cut off rashly, the chapter argues further that even a utility friendship cannot survive one friend's viciousness when the other is virtuous — 'collaboration with corruption corrupts' — so Batman must bury the friendship despite surgery and therapy aimed at restoring the old Dent.

chapters.file: ch60 - The Cop and the Vigilante.md
chapters.relation: Analyzes Batman and Jim Gordon as Aristotle's friendship of utility: the Bat-Signal and police information serve both men's missions, exactly as Bruce's 'I need an inside man' monologue in Batman: Year One intends. The chapter explains why it never deepens into pleasure — Batman's guardedness about his identity and Gordon's doubts about his unpredictability — and shows its fragility: if Batman ever killed, or Gordon had to arrest him, the reciprocity would end. A rebuffed dinner-party invitation dramatizes that they are colleagues 'ultimately no more.'

chapters.file: ch61 - Batman and Catwoman.md
chapters.relation: Classifies Batman's attraction to Catwoman as Aristotle's friendship of pleasure: they relish their bat-and-cat chases, she is neither his mentee nor his colleague, and Aristotle's view that romances are pleasure friendships fits what they have. The chapter argues her underlying goodness — she does not kill and often abandons thefts that could harm Batman — explains the attraction and why, after her reform into a neighborhood protector, Batman finally trusted her with his identity as Bruce Wayne.

chapters.file: ch62 - The Butler and the Man of the Manor.md
chapters.relation: Examines Bruce and Alfred: real mutual utility (Alfred's lifelong service and quasi-parental role against shelter and income), yet Aristotle's requirement of equality blocks complete friendship — Bruce is always the boss and Alfred always the butler, each bound by an overriding sense of mission. The chapter argues any change, Alfred quitting or Bruce dismissing him, would itself be an alienating act of disloyalty, so this closest of relationships is destined never to ascend higher than it stands.

chapters.file: ch63 - The Elusiveness of a Complete Friendship.md
chapters.relation: Argues that Batman himself is chiefly responsible for the elusiveness of complete friendship: the promise to his murdered parents consumes the personal investment such friendship needs, so everyone — Gordon, Dent, the Robins, Batgirl, Alfred — must fit into the mission, as his Hush confession to Catwoman ('I am not very good at this. Having friends.') shows. Aristotle's remark that the good man is a friend to himself lets the chapter cast Bruce and Batman as 'one soul in two personae,' the only virtue friendship left to him. It closes as a cautionary tale: a life of mission can cost the balance — and the friendship — that a good and happy life requires.

chapters.file: ch64 - Chapter 10 - The Fantastic Four as a Family The Strongest Bond of All.md
chapters.relation: Opens Ryall and Tipton's chapter: where most superhero philosophy focuses on the individual choosing to use power for good or evil, Aristotle's insight that we are essentially social creatures directs attention to the philosophically neglected concept of the family. The Fantastic Four are presented as the rare team whose family bonds are as much a part of their story as their adventures.

chapters.file: ch65 - The First Family.md
chapters.relation: Contrasts the Fantastic Four's forty years of continuity with teams like the JLA and Teen Titans who proclaim 'they're family' yet inevitably drift apart. The chapter locates the difference in the blood-and-marriage core (Johnny, Sue, Reed) plus Ben Grimm, whose only tie is friendship with Reed — a friendship tested from the start because Reed's hubris caused the accident that disfigured Ben.

chapters.file: ch66 - Forming Family Bonds.md
chapters.relation: Reads the Fantastic Four's origin through Plato and the 1960s space race: Reed's heedless rush to beat the Russians into space embodies Thrasymachus' Republic claim that the drive for power dominates human life, and Sue shames the reluctant Ben into flying the unshielded ship. Socrates' belief that virtue is its own reward frames the cosmic-ray price each pays — powers eerily matching their personalities — until Ben proposes the team mission statement: 'We've gotta use that power to help mankind, right?'

chapters.file: ch67 - A Partnership for Living Well.md
chapters.relation: The chapter's core argument: Aristotle's Politics defines a city as 'a partnership for living well,' and the family is the most intimate such partnership — the Fantastic Four exemplify it. Ben's loyalty to the friend who disfigured him, serving as Reed's conscience, is explained through all three Aristotelian friendships: utility (the belonging he finds nowhere else, from Avengers stints to wrestling), pleasure (the sibling-style war with Johnny he secretly enjoys), and complete friendship — strongest between Reed and Ben, inseparable from Reed's guilt over the one miracle he cannot perform: restoring his friend's human form.

chapters.file: ch68 - The Family During Turmoil.md
chapters.relation: Surveys the team's turmoil — Ben's walkabouts, Johnny's bids for independence, Reed and Sue's marital strife and suburban experiments, Reed's 'for his own good' secrecy about Ben's cure — to argue that members leave and return not from duty but from a mutual affinity: only within the family do they feel complete and develop their potential best. It also honestly flags the family's dysfunction, reading Ben's departures as a child running away from home and his squabbles with Johnny as sibling rivalry for Reed and Sue's parental attention.

chapters.file: ch69 - The Ethos of Teamwork.md
chapters.relation: Concludes that the Fantastic Four achieve Aristotle's complete friendship and become 'partners for a greater good': unlike Avengers-style teams whose friendships are mainly self-oriented, the Four's bond is unselfish love aiming at the good of the other. The chapter adds that they turn the family's protective instinct outward, so the world's ordinary citizens live like children under their care.

chapters.file: ch70 - Chapter 11 - Comic-Book Wisdom.md
chapters.relation: Opens Michael Thau's chapter: at a time when wisdom seems to have vanished from the culture, real wisdom can still be found embodied and enacted in superhero comics. The chapter will show comics both reflecting the general skepticism about wisdom and offering flashes of genuine appreciation of what wisdom is.

chapters.file: ch71 - Where Has All the Wisdom Gone.md
chapters.relation: Argues that although 'philosopher' means 'lover of wisdom,' wisdom has all but vanished from everyday talk — surviving mostly as the jab 'wise-guy' — and even from philosophy departments, where colleagues are praised as 'clever' or 'brilliant' but never 'wise.' The chapter proposes tracing wisdom's disappearance through comic books, cultural barometers in which superheroes' stories once gave wisdom a recognized place.

chapters.file: ch72 - The Wisdom of Captain Marvel.md
chapters.relation: Shows how natural it was in 1940 to list the wisdom of Solomon first among Captain Marvel's Shazam-granted powers, then examines Geoff Johns' JSA retelling as the modern 'but': Billy Batson's transformation is purely physical, so Solomon's wisdom becomes an external advising voice — a device the chapter compares to the personified Philosophy who visits Boethius in prison. The Stargirl romance dilemma reveals wisdom's advice to break up with Courtney as designed to preserve its own authority — fitting to an admirer of wisdom, yet reading to modern eyes as the self-interested calculation of a skeptical age.

chapters.file: ch73 - Skepticism and Cynicism about Wisdom.md
chapters.relation: Contrasts Earth X, where Odin's wisdom is exposed as a fraud — a frail human ruling an alien race under false pretenses — with Johns' Captain Marvel, which is skeptical without full cynicism. The chapter defends wisdom's advice to Billy as genuinely wise: the detached, larger-temporal-perspective counsel characteristic of the wise in both Western and Eastern traditions, while conceding that modern readers, unlike those of 1940, can no longer be sure the larger picture should trump Courtney's tears and Billy's present feelings.

chapters.file: ch74 - What Wisdom Requires.md
chapters.relation: Explains what wisdom demands: subordinating the loud, here-and-now deliverances of the senses and emotions to reason and the larger picture — as in Plato's wise person contemplating the eternal Forms and the Republic's long course of training, the Bhagavad-Gita's detachment, and Stoic meditative practice. It argues experience is nonetheless central (a sixteen-year-old Captain Marvel could not have it), cites Stick's parting from Matt Murdock in Daredevil over uncontrolled emotion, and uses Casablanca to mark the cultural shift that makes us doubt the larger picture's claims.

chapters.file: ch75 - Our Problems with Wisdom.md
chapters.relation: Diagnoses why we distrust wisdom: unlike the Epicureans, who trained themselves to discern real pleasure beyond immediate sensation — as Spider-Man's self-discipline wins pleasures Peter Parker could not otherwise know — we equate happiness with pleasant sensory experience; and unlike our ancestors, who saw the passions as external forces undermining freedom (Spinoza's bondage of the emotions), we follow Freud's steam-engine model in treating emotional expression as the true self. Material abundance now satisfies the small picture, making skepticism about the larger picture feasible — though, with Socrates, the chapter doubts it has made us any happier.

chapters.file: ch76 - Part Three - Superheroes and Moral Duty.md
ch77 - Chapter 12 - Why Are Superheroes Good Comics and the Ring of Gyges.md
chapters.relation: Opens Jeff Brenzel's chapter: despite philosophers' chatter about Nietzsche's superman, brains in vats, and the trans-human future, academic philosophy has ignored superhero comics — to the loss of a self-declared recovering Silver Age Marvel Maniac. He poses the big question that drives the chapter: why would people with such powers keep choosing to do good and fight evil, at great cost to themselves, for so long?

chapters.file: ch78 - Refining the Question.md
chapters.relation: Refines the question by discarding the definitional answer: Watchmen's Rorschach (whose problematic vigilante motives are bound up with Batman-style justice) and Dr. Manhattan (whose godlike powers shape an alien, morally distant consciousness), together with the Dark Knight and Kingdom Come portrayals, show that even subversive comics presuppose heroes must choose to be good rather than be good by definition.

chapters.file: ch79 - A Genetic Fallacy and Something Too Simple.md
chapters.relation: Disposes of the genetic explanation: the 1954 Comics Code mandated that 'good shall triumph over evil,' but since only a receptive audience kept code-conforming heroes commercially alive, the Code cannot explain why we find super-powered people choosing good plausible and appealing. Stan Lee's reduction of every story to good-guy-vs-bad-guy fights is also too simple — Lee's own humanization of the Fantastic Four and Spider-Man, like Spider-Man 2's near-exclusive focus on Peter's motives, forced the 'extraneous' moral issues to center stage.

chapters.file: ch80 - The Problem with Origins.md
chapters.relation: Argues origin stories function as signs or interpretations of character, not explanations: Bruce Wayne's parents, the Kents' Smallville virtues, and Xavier's gathering of the X-Men inspire but do not determine their choices. Lex Luthor's ludicrous 1960 origin — swearing eternal vengeance on Superboy for accidentally causing his hair loss — is so bad an explanation that it exposes how no single event, in comics or in our confessional talk-show narratives of genetic makeup and upbringing, fixes what we choose to become.

chapters.file: ch81 - Superheroes and the Ring of Gyges.md
chapters.relation: The chapter's heart: Glaucon's Ring of Gyges and 'harsh view' of human nature — justice as the weak's compact against the strong, a lineage running from Hobbes to Nietzsche — are powerfully denied by superheroes and by Frodo, who resist the power of the ring. Socrates' tripartite soul and justice-as-psychic-harmony are read as preparation for the Republic's real answer, the ascent to the eternal Form of the Good, which the chapter extends through Aristotle's teleology and virtue ethics: super-powered people, denied any standard social role, must wrestle with what their potential is for — from Kingdom Come's retired Superman and Spider-Man 2's Peter Parker to Astro City's Samaritan, with Uncle Ben's 'With great power comes great responsibility' as the upshot.

chapters.file: ch82 - Chapter 13 - Why Should Superheroes Be Good Spider-Man, the X-Men, and.md
chapters.relation: Opens C. Stephen Evans' chapter by retelling the Republic's Ring of Gyges passage (359c-360d) — the shepherd who uses invisibility to seduce the king's wife, murder him, and seize the kingdom — as the archetype against which the question 'Why should superheroes be good?' will be posed through Spider-Man, the X-Men, and Kierkegaard's double danger.

chapters.file: ch83 - Plato and the Question of Why We Should Be Good.md
chapters.relation: Reconstructs Glaucon's challenge from the Republic: with a ring making injustice cost-free, no one would keep hands off others' possessions, and anyone who stayed just would be mocked as 'a great fool' behind our self-protective praise; Socrates must show that the truly just person 'stripped of the seeming' — enduring the lash, the rack, and the cross — lives better than the honored unjust one. The chapter then turns Plato's thought-experiment on comic-book worlds: why should someone with superpowers care about being good?

chapters.file: ch84 - Kierkegaard and the Concept of the “Double Danger”.md
chapters.relation: Introduces Kierkegaard's Works of Love: called to universal neighbor-love, we face a 'double danger' — first the inner struggle against selfishness and inertia, then, once we make headway, the world's persecution of genuine goodness, as happened to Socrates, Jesus, and (in his lifetime) Martin Luther King. Genuine self-denial means working unselfishly for the good and then 'being abominated almost as a criminal' for it, a theme the chapter finds explored in Busiek and Ross' Marvels — while Superman, with his undoubting character and public acclaim, faces neither danger.

chapters.file: ch85 - Spider-Man’s Struggles.md
chapters.relation: Shows Spider-Man living both of Kierkegaard's dangers: the first as his love for Mary Jane collides with his vocation — missing her play in Spider-Man 2, then throwing away the costume — though Peter is tempted to be ordinary, never evil, refuting Glaucon's prediction about the powerful. The second appears in J. Jonah Jameson's newsroom, which spins Spider-Man's good deeds into menace, the discomfort with super-powered goodness Kierkegaard predicted ordinary people would feel.

chapters.file: ch86 - The X-Men and the Double Danger.md
chapters.relation: Applies the double danger to the X-Men: feared and hated as mutants, with Senator Kelly's registration laws disturbingly recalling Nazi measures against Jews, they are split between Xavier's inclusive peace and Magneto's war on humanity — proof the choice of good is not automatic even for them. Wolverine's growth from rage into Xavier's moral community dramatizes the inner first danger, while their persecution despite unconditional, universal neighbor-love dramatizes the second — including the extra resentment earned by demonstrating their persecutors' irrationality.

chapters.file: ch87 - Why Are the X-Men Good.md
chapters.relation: Systematically rejects candidate explanations of the X-Men's goodness: not self-interested calculation (the world's hostility undercuts it, blunting Magneto's argument), not innate constitution (Magneto chose otherwise, and the Cyclops–Wolverine–Jean Grey triangle shows ordinary desires), not fear of punishment, and not Nietzschean pity or herd resentment — the X-Men are the strong and healthy ones. The chapter's positive account: love of the good is learned through relationships with those who are good to us, from Xavier's loving school that gradually transforms Wolverine and Magneto's Nazi-scarred past to Peter Parker's formative upbringing by Uncle Ben and Aunt May.

chapters.file: ch88 - Finding a Strong Basis for the Good.md
chapters.relation: Argues that loving role models give a motivation but not yet a reason to be good, available to everyone: Plato grounds goodness in a universe whose deep character is just — a metaphysical vision Augustine and C.S. Lewis found religiously congenial — while Kierkegaard grounds the duty of neighbor-love in our relationship to the God who created us out of nothing for eternal life, whose love shown in Christ lets even the persecuted face the double danger with hope. The chapter ends by noting the puzzling absence of religion from the X-Men's world: were its homo religiosus inhabitants to ask what universe they inhabit, they might find in loving the neighbor their deepest connection to the One who perfectly loves them.

chapters.file: ch89 - Chapter 14 - With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility On the Moral Duties.md
chapters.relation: Opens Christopher Robichaud's chapter with the midpoint of Spider-Man 2: Peter quits, crime in New York rises seventy-five percent, and unable to walk down the street without meeting someone who needs Spider-Man, he asks 'What am I supposed to do?' — the normative question of what duties, if any, come with great power.

chapters.file: ch90 - With Great Power Comes—What.md
chapters.relation: Turns Uncle Ben's dictum into normative ethics: the question is not how super-powered people do live but how they ought to, whether they have a duty to take up the hero role, and what obligations follow from it. Two 'hobgoblins' — ethical nihilism and ethical relativism — are dismissed as contrary to our ordinary convictions (Mother Teresa's charity objectively good, Hitler's genocide absolutely bad), clearing the ground for utilitarianism.

chapters.file: ch91 - Start Stitchin’ That Costume, Bub. Duty Calls.md
chapters.relation: Explains Mill-style utilitarianism — rightness fixed entirely by consequences for overall pleasure and pain, counting every sentient being (a cat may enjoy tuna but not Watchmen) — and applies it: Clark Kent must rescue the failing plane over the Daily Planet press conference, and you must give the jeans money to charity. Since adopting a role is obligated whenever it produces the most overall good, anyone with superpowers has a duty to become a superhero, so Peter Parker's misery in Spider-Man 2 is morally beside the point: utilitarianism says he must remain Spider-Man.

chapters.file: ch92 - Aw, C’mon! Do I Have to Save the Day.md
chapters.relation: Presses four objections to utilitarianism through superhero cases: a weakened Jean Grey dying to save Juggernaut's bus victims shows utilitarianism obliterates supererogation — she would be blameworthy whichever way she chose; Ares' demand that Wonder Woman kill an innocent girl to avert global biowar forces her against her character; Batman refusing to let an innocent-of-this-crime Joker die in The Joker: Devil's Advocate shows the theory sacrificing justice; and the Green Goblin accidentally doing great good by dragging a would-be mass shooter down Fifth Avenue shows consequences alone cannot make an intended wrong right.

chapters.file: ch93 - I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!.md
chapters.relation: Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.

holes.name: Moral Perfectionism (the exemplar and the higher self)
holes.what: A moral viewpoint on which the ethical life is the quest to become a higher self, guided by exemplars who acknowledge and legitimate one's aspiration rather than dictate conformity.
holes.why: Chapters 53-55 read Batgirl: Year One and Oracle entirely through moral perfectionism (Nietzsche's 'Schopenhauer as Educator', Mill on individuality), a framework taxonomy lacks; ch53 introduces it via Barbara Gordon's quest for Batman's acknowledgment.

holes.name: Wisdom (sophia, the larger picture)
holes.what: The classical ideal of wisdom: seeing the larger picture by training reason, through experience and meditative discipline, to master the pull of the senses and emotions on action.
holes.why: Book chapters 70-75 are all about the nature, training, and modern disappearance of wisdom (Solomon to Stoics); taxonomy has only Aristotle's narrower phronesis, not wisdom as such.

holes.name: The Double Danger (Works of Love)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's account of the moral/Christian life as a double struggle: inward against selfishness, and outward against a world that persecutes and ridicules genuine neighbor-love.
holes.why: Chapter 84 introduces the double danger from Works of Love and chapters 85-88 apply it to Spider-Man and the X-Men; no existing Kierkegaard slug covers neighbor-love or the double danger.

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Actions that are praiseworthy to do but not wrong to omit — above and beyond what duty requires.
holes.why: Chapter 92 argues utilitarianism cannot accommodate supererogatory acts (Jean Grey's sacrifice) and chapter 93 concludes that being a superhero is precisely such a supererogatory choice; the concept is absent from taxonomy.
